title: Clerkship at Lund University -LAGOM- and at the University of Pittsburgh
paragraphs: This time I spent four weeks at Lund University in Sweden, and then about four weeks at the Infectious Diseases department and infectious diseases laboratory of the University of Pittsburgh, where Dr. 土井, an alumnus of the Frontier Society, works.

For Sweden, I had originally planned two months, April and May, but because of circumstances on the Lund University side it became April only. This year was the first time anyone was sent to Lund University, so preparing for study abroad was a matter of feeling my way, but the doctors of the International Collaboration Office and the staff of the office over there treated me kindly and carefully, and I was able to finish my study abroad without trouble. Students of Lund University who had previously come to Nagoya University to study also helped me sincerely and were a great support. My clerkship department at Lund University was general surgery. It was subdivided further, and I did my clerkship in the field of the lower gastrointestinal tract, in colorectal surgery. The clerkship consisted of rounds, outpatient clinic, surgery (scrubbing in) and conferences, and there was much that I was allowed to do, such as procedures during rounds and retracting and suturing in the surgical field, and in free time young doctors in the position of fellows sometimes gave mini-lectures. My overall impression was that many people worked cheerfully, and I felt that the mental leeway may come precisely because they value their private lives. A female doctor who looked after me constantly joked with colleagues and patients, and smiles never left the people around her. Once, a patient who had shut himself in his room from postoperative distress and had lost even the energy to eat got his smile, appetite and motivation back thanks to her talk.

Sweden is a non-English-speaking country, and I dove in with both anticipation and anxiety about that, but in Sweden, said to have the best English of the non-English-speaking countries, everyone spoke English so well that I felt no difficulty in communicating. However, many older patients were not good at English, so I could not ask for the outpatient clinic to be in English. Still, I got the impression that if I did a clerkship in a department with young patients, I might perhaps be able to take simple histories. The doctors also looked out for me, holding conferences and chats in English, and in the outpatient clinic, after communicating with the patient, explaining to me in English. I had also bought something like a simple Swedish conversation book in Japan before departure and studied a little, but I felt it was nowhere near enough and that I wished I could speak more, so I bought a mini English-Swedish dictionary small enough to fit in a scrub pocket locally and carried it with me during the clerkship and in private. In the outpatient clinic in particular, it was a chance to listen to plenty of Swedish, so I picked up words I knew while reading the context, and checked words I did not know in the dictionary from their pronunciation. Since I shared a room with two Lund University students, after getting home I would ask them, "Today in this kind of situation I heard a word that sounded like this, what does it mean?" Because my base Swedish was low, it was fun that the words I knew and could catch increased, and when I actually used it myself the doctors praised me, saying I had gotten good, so it was a very good environment for language acquisition. In that sense too, I felt I wished I could have stayed for two months.

As for life, Swedish students mostly start living alone or sharing a room with friends after finishing high school, and Lund University also offers many student dormitories with various room types. Students' extracurricular activities are also lively, and student clubs called Nations organize lunches and drinking parties two or three times a week, and the Mentor Group for international students and the International Buddy Group (for the medical school) organized events such as hiking, so it was an environment where there were various choices for how to spend weekday evenings and weekends. Also, Sweden is a high-welfare country with high taxes, and I received a mild culture shock when I heard that you can feel that the taxes you pay are returned to the people and used for good things, so you pay gladly no matter how high they are! Seeing doctors at my clerkship site, men and women alike, taking leave or leaving early because their child was unwell, continuing to receive a certain salary during maternity and parental leave, and not paying school fees or medical costs for children, I felt that the whole country is kind to children and child rearing. They apparently also have the problem of a high divorce rate as a result, however.

In June I went to the University of Pittsburgh in Pennsylvania in the United States. I toured the laboratory and, thanks to Dr. 土井's consideration, was also able to visit the Infectious Diseases department. In the morning, together with medical students and residents, I attended an hour-long lecture on a different topic each day given by the fellows. After that I took part in the conference, follow-up of existing patients, presentations of newly consulted patients, and rounds. It was very educational because in my clerkships in Japan I had never rotated for a long period specializing in infectious diseases, and because I was able to see and hear infectious diseases peculiar to North America and ones I had not known in Japan. Coming into contact with the doctors' logical way of thinking was also a good experience. In the laboratory, the researchers and students welcomed me warmly, introduced their respective research, did experiments with me and read papers together, which was educational. It was also interesting to attend ASM Microbe, a microbiology and infectious diseases conference with more than 10,000 participants.

In these roughly two months I was able to have truly many meaningful experiences. I have been living with the wish to challenge various things and broaden my world and perspective while a student, so I am very glad to have had this kind of experience in my last year as a student. I express my deep gratitude to everyone who gave me the opportunity and supported me. Thank you very much.
